**Shingo Kunieda** (国枝 慎吾 _Kunieda Shingo_ ; born February 21, 1984) is a Japanese former [wheelchair tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis "Wheelchair tennis") player. With four [Paralympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis_at_the_Summer_Paralympics "Wheelchair tennis at the Summer Paralympics") gold medals, 28 [major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Slam_\(tennis\)#Tournaments "Grand Slam \(tennis\)") singles titles – an [all-time record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Grand_Slam%E2%80%93related_tennis_records "List of Grand Slam–related tennis records") in singles of any tennis discipline – and 50 major titles overall, Kunieda is widely considered the greatest male wheelchair player of all time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-2)
Kunieda was the ITF World Champion from 2007 to 2010. He was also the year-end No. 1 in doubles in 2007. In 2007, 2009, 2010, 2014, and 2015, Kunieda won all three singles majors that hosted wheelchair singles events ([Wimbledon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Championships,_Wimbledon "The Championships, Wimbledon") did not do so until [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Wimbledon_Championships "2016 Wimbledon Championships")). In 2007 and 2008, Kunieda also won three of the four Masters series events. Kunieda is the only male player to retain the men's singles title at the Paralympics – he took the gold medal in [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis_at_the_2008_Summer_Paralympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_singles "Wheelchair tennis at the 2008 Summer Paralympics – Men's singles"), [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis_at_the_2012_Summer_Paralympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_singles "Wheelchair tennis at the 2012 Summer Paralympics – Men's singles") and [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis_at_the_2020_Summer_Paralympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_singles "Wheelchair tennis at the 2020 Summer Paralympics – Men's singles"). In addition, Kunieda won the gold medal in the [2004 men's doubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_tennis_at_the_2004_Summer_Paralympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_doubles "Wheelchair tennis at the 2004 Summer Paralympics – Men's doubles"), and has been part of two World Team Cup wins. He has 103 career titles over singles and doubles combined, including 50 majors.
Kunieda had a three-year, 106-match consecutive win streak. The streak began after his loss at the 2007 Masters and ended to [Stéphane Houdet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Houdet "Stéphane Houdet") in the semifinals of the 2010 Masters.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-3) In late 2012 to early 2013, Kunieda had a win streak of 44 matches. Between January 2014 and December 2015, Kunieda was on yet another winning streak of 77 matches, ending to [Joachim Gérard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_G%C3%A9rard "Joachim Gérard") in the round-robin phase of the 2015 NEC Masters tournament.
Kunieda is a right-handed player whose favorite surface is [hard court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_court "Hard court").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was coached by Hiromichi Maruyama. He announced his retirement in January 2023.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-itftennis.com-4)
## Biography
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shingo_Kunieda&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]
Due to a tumor in his spinal cord found when he was 9, he is paralyzed in the lower half of his body. Kunieda uses an Ox Engineering wheelchair. He graduated from [Reitaku University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reitaku_University "Reitaku University") in Japan, and now works for Reitaku University.

In these years, Kunieda dominated the world of men's singles wheelchair events. In 2013, he started off by winning the APIA Sydney International Wheelchair Open. Then, he won his eighth Australian Open at the [2013 Australian Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Australian_Open "2013 Australian Open"), by beating [Stéphane Houdet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%A9phane_Houdet "Stéphane Houdet") in the final. At the BNP Paribas 2013 Team World Cup, Kunieda won 2 out of 3 matches, including a Group 1 win over Stéphane Houdet.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-102) At the [2013 French Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_French_Open "2013 French Open"), Kunieda reached his sixth final at the event, but lost to Stéphane Houdet in three tight sets.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-103)
### 2021–2023 Non calendar year Grand Slam and retirement
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shingo_Kunieda&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2021–2023 Non calendar year Grand Slam and retirement")]
In the Tokyo Paralympics, which was held in 2021 due to COVID-19, Kunieda won five matches without dropping a set to win gold in the singles. The semifinal win was against defending champion Reid and the final was against Egberink.
In the US Open Kunieda beat Ratzlaff, Reid and Hewett to win his 25th major singles title.
In the 2022 Australian Open Kunieda beat Gérard and Egberink to reach the final. In the final Kunieda beat Hewett 7–5, 3–6, 6–2.
In the 2022 French Open Kunieda beat Houdet and Oda to reach the final. In the final he beat Fernandez 6–2, 5–7, 7–5.
In the 2022 Wimbledon Championships Kunieda beat Egberink and defending champion Gérard to reach the final. In the final he faced Hewett. Kunieda lost the first set 4–6 but won the second set 7–5.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-WM_2022-104) In the deciding set Kunieda was 2–5 down and Hewett served for the championship four times.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-WM_2022-104) Despite this Kunieda won the deciding set 7–6 after winning the super tiebreaker 10–5. Victory meant that Kunieda had won the non calendar year Grand Slam and career Super Slam in the singles.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-WM_2022-104) This was his 28th major singles title. In the doubles Kunieda and his partner Fernandez beat defending champions Hewett and Reid 6–3, 6–1 in the final to end Hewett and Reid's streak of 10 major titles.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-WM_2022-104)
In the 2022 US Open Kunieda was hoping to win the Grand Slam. He beat Gérard, de la Puenta and Miki to reach the final. In the final he lost 6–7, 1–6 to Hewett.
He announced his retirement in January 2023.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-itftennis.com-4)
## Playing style
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Shingo_Kunieda&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Playing style")]
Overwhelming "chair work" is a strength. Wheelchair tennis is allowed up to two bounces, but Kunieda hits almost all balls with one bounce. For opponents, it is a threat because the time to wait for the ball is halved. In 2008 former world No. 3 Michael Jeremias also said, "It's true that he has almighty abilities, but what he excels at is his speed of movement. He is outstanding in the current world of wheelchair tennis."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-Chair_work-105) Service and backhand have also been improved according to the times and injuries.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-Super_athlete-106)
Until 2006, he was ranked around 10th in the world, but with the advice of Anne Quinn, a mental trainer he met at the Australian Open, he started saying "I'm the strongest!" The face was strengthened[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-Super_athlete-106) and after 10 months he became world rank 1.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shingo_Kunieda#cite_note-\(38\)_World_Champion-107)
